newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia killer storm death toll rises to 125.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia killer storm death toll rises to 125.

text.p: The death toll from Malaysia's Christmas Day storm rose to 125 as rescuers stepped up their search for at least 100 people still believed missing, officials said on Saturday.

Police said 112 bodies were found in the logging town of Keningau, the worst affected area in eastern Sabah state, the national Bernama news agency reported. Other bodies were found in the neighbouring towns of Papar, Tuaran and Kota Kinabalu.
The death toll was expected to rise after three days of searching for those missing, officials said.

Tropical storm Greg, which blew ashore from the South China Sea at 70 kph (44 mph) on Wednesday, triggered heavy rains and floods which swelled rivers to overflowing, downed power lines and washed out road and communications links.
Keningau, a small logging town 150 km (95 miles) south of Sabah state capital Kota Kinabalu, bore the brunt of the floods.
Officials said 500 houses in nine villages along four rivers in the town were washed away. Bernama said nearly 7,000 people had been moved to temporary shelters because of the storm.
Villagers have started to clean up a mountain of debris which engulfed their houses, buried cars and washed out roads.
Officials, who said most of the dead were Indonesian migrant workers, blamed the building of houses close to riverbanks and illegal logging as among reasons for the high casualty rate.
The storm alert system also needed improving, Malaysian Information Minister Mohamed Rahmat was quoted as saying by local newspapers on Saturday.

In his first comments on the storm, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Saturday that priority should be given to relief work instead of trying to determine who was at fault for the tragedy. "I think it is better for us to learn from the incident than to be quick to blame others," Mahathir told reporters at the northern island of Langkawi.

"Although we have the ability to make weather forecasts, the predictions were often not precise enough, especially regarding their impact," he said in reference to criticisms that the Meteorological Department did not warn about the scale of the storm.
He dismissed suggestions that Malaysia could not cope with disasters like the one in Sabah.
"We are actually prepared to face disasters. But even a developed country like Japan could not prevent the earthquake that devastated Kobe," he said.

Science, Technology and Environment Minister Law Hieng Ding told reporters that Sabah and Sarawak will be given two extra weather radars to add to the two existing ones to improve weather forecast in the two Borneo states.
